title: Canto Four. The Marriage
html:
Beginning of studies, upanayana, study under Gangadasa; the Lord teaches bhakti and introduces vows; Vishvarupa's return and departure (Shankararanya); the swoon after betel; the passing of Jagannatha Mishra; the marriage with Lakshmipriya; the beauty of young Gaura (pp. 20–23)

[p. 20]

1And now He, adorned with the beauty of boyhood polished by good upbringing, with golden, tender, lovely limbs — after His father had performed for Him the tonsure and other rites — on a certain day, under favourable Jupiter, Moon, asterism and Sun, began to learn His letters.

2Holding hard chalk in His little hand, the Lord, eloquent in all the sciences, began to write on the ground, made bright by the gleam of His gold ornaments, the letters — vowels and consonants — in order.

3The king of the twice-born on earth [Mishra] performed the upanayana of his son, of sweetest form and great glory, who had reached the middle of boyhood — in the fifth season of the year, [counting] from the rains — with unsurpassed rites and festivities with alms for the poor.1

4Having grasped within a few days the secret of the rows of words, He — wishing to master the science that [for others] requires long study — went with His father, bearing gifts, to the great teacher Gangadasa to study grammar.

5Following the teacher's word, His mind intent on listening, instructed only once, without effort, He learned and began to expound the beautiful Kalapa grammar with its terms, sandhi, nouns, verbs and meanings.2

6Then within a few days, having become expert in sutras and commentaries, having learned poetry, the Shruti and the science of ornaments of speech, having studied the great Bhashya too, He took a liking to Nyaya, Vaisheshika and the other sciences.

7As a helmsman effortlessly brings a sturdy ship, driven by a favourable wind, to shore, so the teacher swiftly brought this Supreme Person to the far shore of the ocean of the various sciences — and reached it himself.

8From then on the Lord, establishing that the injunctions [of scripture] speak of devotion to Vishnu, and showing its distinction as the supreme goal from karma, knowledge, yoga and the rest, became a teacher in all lands.

9Even His chatter, usually like the Vedas and faultless, no one would contravene; only the heretic bent on hell did not honour it — as a dying man rejects medicine.

10Wishing to raise up the fierce hordes of heretics on earth walking a false path by the law of the Lord-Protector, He introduced vows for Hari's appearance day and other [festivals], for the ekadashis of Kartika, and arranged festivities.

11One day He, a moon among the host of sages, lovingly and humbly induced His mother to observe fasts and vows on the days of the Conqueror of the Daityas; and Mishra, delighted, began to do the same.3

12Some days later the peaceful Vishvarupa, having ascertained the descent of the Lord and wishing to see His incomparably beautiful form, unexpectedly entered his father's town in the dress of a brahmachari.

13Seeing him, the people there thought he had returned from another world and rejoiced greatly; and Mishra, with his [younger] son, brought him into his house.

14Joyfully feeding him various sweet dishes and constantly caring for him, beautiful as Kama, Mishra after some time thought it fitting for the youth to marry.

15Learning of his father's intention, Vishvarupa soon, addressing Vishvambhara in private, said to Him: "You are the Lord of the world; purify the people who cling to deceptive family life by bestowing prema-bhakti upon them."

[p. 21]

16Having somehow told Him this in secret, he embraced Him tightly in great love and, quick of mind, left fearlessly at night while the whole world slept — [taking] the name Shankararanya.4

17When this son — pure, beautiful in body, of pure character and brief [household] life — had left the house, Mishra and Shachi, stricken with grief, bereft of all joy, wept aloud.

18To console them, the magnanimous One said to His parents: "Why do you weep for a son who has gone forth to wander? He has become a purifier of the whole world, and of us too; for no one grieves over a son who has become a lord of the earth.

19And I will serve you here, venerable ones — with food, clothing, bedding, oil massage and ointments for the whole body. This is the happiness that parents receive from a son; with many sons one is not the happier — such is the rule."

20When the lovely son, casting off grief, spoke thus, they, beloved of their kin, regained their joy; and the Lord, captivating with His charm, in the full beauty of boyhood, devoted Himself to serving His parents' feet.

21Once, having eaten at home a roll of betel — the remnant [of an offering] to the chosen Deity, prepared by His own hand — the Lord suddenly fainted; coming round from the sprinkling of water from a fan and His mother's tears, He said:

22"Mother, listen to Me: Vishvarupa told Me to renounce all this at once and leave. And I answered him: 'That is not fitting for us now: we are engaged in serving our father's feet.'

23Hearing My words, he, full of deep love, at once pressed Me to his heart, embraced Me and said: 'Ah, dear one, on the path ordained by destiny, convey to father and mother my repeated obeisances.'

24Having drunk his words like nectar — now, mother, that the bewilderment has passed, I know: 'I am he.' Where has my loving brother gone again? What is this?" — and in confusion He fainted again at once.5

25Hearing these words of his son, whose greatness is inconceivable — [entering] his ears [and full of the meaning] of hundreds of Shrutis — Mishra thought: "He is the One who does even this, for His will is always fulfilled. Hari, Hari! What is this that has suddenly happened?" — and grew sad.

26From that time, indifferent to sense objects, constantly contemplating Adhokshaja beyond the world, expecting nothing, his karma exhausted by austerity, he left his emaciated body and attained a form of bliss.6

27When the father had departed, He, bathed in streams of tears — alas! — began to lament loudly and piteously; and Shachi, seeing her son's grief, her grief for her husband doubled, wept aloud like an osprey.

28With their loud weeping, with cries of "ah, ah!" and with the tears of relatives and friends, the whole town was filled; people sank [into grief] as into a deep ocean — while the Lord for a moment became as one standing on the shore.

29The townspeople, coming to Mishra's house, wept with them on the way and there; but some steadfast ones, gathering their strength, soon consoled with their counsel the excellent Lord together with His mother.

30Then, to show what befits a son, the Lord of the world, in play, performed all the rites for His father. He is the abode of all, His desires ever fulfilled; and that one [the father], as the father of Hari, shines as eternally liberated.7

31Then, having duly performed the shraddha for His father together with all His friends, relatives and kinsmen, He enjoyed [life], surrounded by the retinue of the beauty of youth (kaishora), full of the play of love — as though by a great coronation.

32Then the skilful and resourceful Vanamali, noticing that Shachi was intent on her son's marriage, displayed the adroitness that is [still] spoken of in connection with the Lord's wedding — [proposing] the daughter of Vallabhacharya.

[p. 22]

33Having ascertained the standing of both families and consulted once more with Srivasa and other devotees, on a favourable day, together with assembled relatives and friends, they performed the rite of the binding word — the betrothal of bride and groom.

34Before the wedding, to the loud sound of trumpets, the blessings of brahmins, dancing, singing and the rest, Gaurachandra with the best of His clan, seated in splendid palanquins, and with the townspeople set out for His father-in-law's town.

35Vallabha himself with his people came out to meet Him, who arrived with His relatives and in-laws; on the road the two parties met — a joy like the meeting of moon and ocean at the full moon.

36Vallabha, versed in the Rigveda, having done everything according to rule, led the groom, the best of gods, to the altar, seated Him, washed His feet and honoured Him with a large golden seat, a grass mat and the other six gifts to a guest.

37Bringing to Him his daughter, adorned with new clothes and ornaments — Lakshmi, incomparable among the young maidens of the world — he gave her to Him with a manifold dowry, as Himavat gave his daughter to Shiva.

38Hari, pleased, took her hand in His, completed the remaining rites with the experts in wedding rites and, regaled with His wife and companions with delicious food — payasa, cakes, soups — stayed there.

39The night, lovely with moonlight, desired by lovers, which had soothed the heat of day, lit by many lamps, uprooting lovers' pique with loud coaxing songs of Kama —

40that night, giver of various joys, He spent there with friends on many couches soft as moonlight, in merry talk and sleep.

41When in the sky, as in a lake cleared of the mud of darkness, where the star-fishes had hidden, the swan [-sun] rose, eager for play — the buds of Hari's lotus eyes opened, and the dawn surely attained a pure autumnal beauty.

42By the harsh cawing of crows, by the coolness of the touch of pearls, by the red glow in the east, by the bitterness of betel remnants, by the scent of opening lotuses, the people there — through their senses — at once understood in their hearts that morning had come.

43Then the Lord, seating in front in an auspicious palanquin His beloved, Vallabha's daughter, with dancing and the like, set out for His own town as before, having satisfied His father-in-law and gladly accepted his gifts.

44[She] entered the town — with lofty towers touching the clouds, girt with walls, with rich markets, with inner apartments full of noble ladies, with borders washed by the waves of the celestial river.

45Sri Shachi meekly approached her daughter-in-law, the incomparable beauty of the three worlds, who bowed before her, and embraced her; and seeing her son, who had found a worthy wife, bowing too, she attained great joy in the world of men.8

46Thus, when Hari, noble in deeds, had taken a wife, and His boyhood with its fierce lustre was gradually coming to an end, in the sky of His body the moon of youth rose — beautiful, of fathomless charm, maddening men, enlivening a new art of graceful movements.

47His feet [stole the beauty] of the red lotus, His knees — of a pair [of plantain trunks (?)], His thighs — of an elephant-post, His broad hips — of a pair of gourds, His waist — of the lion, His navel — of a whirlpool, His chest — of a door, His arms — of the trunks of lordly elephants, His neck — of the conch,

[p. 23]

48His lips — of the bimba fruit, the row of His teeth — of pearls, His nose — of a freshly opened sesame flower, His eyes — of a pair of lotuses, His face — of the moon, His hair — of a dark chamara: all these limbs of the Lord, robbing them of their beauty, left everything else bereft of charm.9

49Once this Hari, enchanting the hosts of gods and asuras in the form of Mohini, distributed the essence of nectar separately to the beautiful gods; now He has appeared again on earth, distributing the nectar of bhava to the devotees — "Is this not Mohini in male form?" — so people thought of Him then.10

50In the Sri Gaura-krishnodaya, composed for the delight of connoisseurs by Govinda — a bee intoxicated by tasting the drops of honey that open within the lotus feet of Sri Gauranga, the bull among the lords of sannyasis — the fourth canto, flowing freely in verse and full of power, has come to its close.

Thus ends the fourth canto of the Sri Gaura-krishnodaya composed by Sri Govinda, named "The Marriage Performed."

Notes

  1. The beginning of studies (hate-khari) and the upanayana — CC Adi 14–15. Vārṣikāt pañcamartau, "in the fifth season from the rains": rains, autumn, hemanta, shishira, spring — i.e. in spring (vasanta), the prescribed time for a brahmin's upanayana ("in spring let him initiate a brahmin").
  2. The Kalapa (Katantra) is the grammar studied in Bengal. Study under Gangadasa Pandita — CC Adi 15. In v. 4 (checked against the scan) the words cira-sahacara-vidyā-bhaṅga-pāraṅgahamohasau are so printed and unclear (probably corrupt); we translate by the sense. Śava-śāstra is a misprint for śabda-śāstra, "grammar".
  3. CC Adi 15: the Lord asked His mother not to eat grains on ekadashi, and from then on she kept the fast. In Govinda-deva, also the introduction of Janmashtami and the Kartika vows.
  4. Govinda-deva's own version. In the CC (Adi 15) Vishvarupa leaves home on learning that his parents intend to marry him — once and for all; in Govinda-deva he first became a monk (1.59–60), and now returns, stays at home and leaves again when his father plans his marriage. The sannyasa name Shankararanya — CC Adi 13 (Vishvarupa took sannyasa and under this name later left the world at Pandharpur, Madhya 9).
  5. CC Adi 15: the Lord, after eating betel, fainted, and on coming to Himself said that Vishvarupa had called Him to take sannyasa, but He had refused for the sake of serving His parents, and Vishvarupa sent his respects to the parents. The words "I am he" (so 'ham asmi) do not here carry the Mayavadi sense of identifying the soul with Brahman: they mean that the departed brother is now non-different from the Lord — cf. 1.42, 1.59 (Vishvarupa is Vishnu, present within the Lord); according to the tradition followed by Bhaktisiddhanta, Vishvarupa after his departure entered Nityananda.
  6. The passing of Jagannatha Mishra — CC Adi 15 (briefly). Its connection with grief over Vishvarupa's departure is Govinda-deva's.
  7. "The father of Hari": Jagannatha Mishra is, according to the GGD, Nanda Maharaja (cf. 1.41) — an eternal associate of the Lord, not a conditioned soul liberated by means of the rite. In the second half of the verse (checked against the scan) ayam akhila-nivāso nitya-pūrṇābhilāṣaḥ, "He is the abode of all, His desires ever fulfilled", is said of the Lord: He needs no rites and performs them in play; sa hi hari-janakatvān nitya-mukto vibhāti is said of the father.
  8. Vanamali Acharya's matchmaking and the marriage with Lakshmipriya — CC Adi 15 (briefly), in detail CB, Adi-khanda. In Govinda-deva the groom travels with a wedding procession to his father-in-law's town.
  9. A traditional "head-to-foot" description of beauty (nakha-shikha), built on the image of "stealing" beauty from the objects of comparison. In v. 47 (checked against the scan) the comparison for the knees is printed raṇḍayoḥ, an unclear word (perhaps a misprint for rambhayoḥ, "of two plantain trunks"); the rendering is conjectural.
  10. Mohini is the female avatara of Vishnu who distributed the nectar to the gods at the churning of the ocean (Bhag. 8.8–9). Cf. the CC: the Lord distributes the nectar of prema that had never been given before.
